name: Injuries: What to Stockpile, Who to Trust
author: Dr. Anonymous
description: A practical medical preparation guide circulated through freelancer networks in the GLMZ the Gray Zone and Narrows districts, authored by someone with evident clinical training operating outside licensed practice. Written in plain language with specific drug names, triage logic, and sourcing advice for off-books care. Copies have been found in C-tier dead drops, tucked into broker packets, and photographed on the Gray Zone bulletin boards. The author is unknown; the handwriting on early versions suggests multiple transcriptions from an original oral source.
body:
INJURIES: WHAT TO STOCKPILE, WHO TO TRUST
A guide for people who cannot walk into a clinic

I'm going to assume you're reading this because you already know why you can't go to a registered MedFac. Maybe Arcturus has a flag on your biometrics. Maybe you're carrying three outstanding contractor violations and the moment a nurse waves a scanner near your wrist, you're detained. Maybe you just can't afford the access tier and you never could.

I'm not here to tell you the system is broken. You know that. I'm here to keep you alive long enough to be angry about it later.

---

THE FIRST HOUR: WHAT KILLS YOU FAST

Arterial bleeding. You have roughly three to six minutes if a major artery is cut and you do nothing. The femoral is the one that gets freelancers most often — inner thigh, mid-leg, feels like pressure more than pain at first because of adrenaline. You won't feel how bad it is. That's the problem.

Every kit needs a tourniquet. Not a belt. Not a strip of fabric. A proper ratcheting tourniquet — Harken makes a decent one, the HTQ-7, you can find them at any gray market supply house or through broker networks for around Φ40. Apply it two finger-widths above the wound, tighten until bleeding stops, note the time on your overlay or write it on your own skin if you have to. Limb loss becomes likely after two hours. That's your window.

For wounds you can't tourniquet — neck, groin crease, axilla — you need a hemostatic packing agent. Clotpak is the common brand name; the active compound is zeolite-accelerated chitosan. You pack the wound, you apply direct pressure for a minimum of three minutes, you don't lift the dressing to check. I know you want to check. Don't check.

Tension pneumothorax. If someone takes a penetrating chest wound and starts to deteriorate — gets worse instead of better, neck veins standing out, trachea shifting, breathing stops helping — that's not a wound you can fix with gauze. You need needle decompression. Second intercostal space, midclavicular line, large-bore needle or a purpose-made device (NeedEx makes a spring-loaded version that doesn't require you to know what you're doing). This saves lives. It also requires practice. Find a broker who can connect you to someone willing to teach it. It's worth the cost.

Anaphylaxis. Some augmentation rejection responses present like anaphylaxis. So does actual anaphylaxis. Epi-dose auto-injectors, brand name Rapidin, outer thigh, hold for ten seconds. Keep two. Tolerance builds in heavy aug users; you may need both.

---

WHAT CAN WAIT (AND WHAT ONLY FEELS LIKE IT CAN)

Can wait, with proper field management: lacerations that aren't arterial, closed fractures of non-axial bones, burns under fifteen percent body surface area, dislocations if you know what you're doing.

Feels like it can wait but will kill you: puncture wounds to the abdomen. Any abdominal penetration — knife, spike, low-velocity fragment — can feel manageable for twelve to thirty-six hours while peritonitis develops. By the time you feel sick, you're in serious trouble. Signs: fever climbing past 38.5, rigid abdomen, pain that gets worse instead of better. This is the one that sends freelancers to real clinics regardless of the consequences, and rightly so.

Infection. Wounds in the Gray Zone environments carry heavy contamination loads. Anything that's been open more than six hours and wasn't immediately cleaned needs antibiotic coverage. Broadex (broad-spectrum oral, covers most common wound pathogens) is available through gray market pharmacies — ask specifically, don't accept substitutes from people who don't know what the substitutes are. Standard course: seven days, complete the course even if it feels better. Stopping early breeds resistance in your own wound and in the networks you share space with.

Concussion with loss of consciousness. If someone was out for any period, watch them for four hours minimum. Nausea, confusion, pupils that don't match, declining coherence — these are signs of intracranial bleed. There is nothing you can do for that in the field. Get them to care.

---

BUILDING A KIT ON A C-TIER BUDGET

Target Φ200-300 assembled over time. Priority order:

1. HTQ-7 tourniquet or equivalent (Φ40)
2. Clotpak hemostatic dressing, two units (Φ30 each)
3. Rapidin epi-dose injectors, two (Φ25 each, prescription-listed but available gray)
4. Broadex antibiotic course, two cycles (Φ20 each)
5. Irrigation syringe and saline solution — 500mL minimum. Clean wounds with volume and pressure. This is more important than antiseptic.
6. Steri-close adhesive strips and staple closure kit
7. NeedEx chest decompression unit (Φ60 — worth it)
8. Burn gel packets, Calmex brand
9. Ibuprofen plus codeine compound for pain — Dullox is the common name, gray market
10. Oral rehydration salts. Cheap. People forget. Shock and blood loss both dehydrate you.

Store in a waterproof case. Know where it is. Tell one person you trust where it is.

---

AUGMENTATION INJURIES

This deserves its own section because chrome and organic wounds behave differently and treating them the same will hurt you.

An augmentation injury — partial crush of a chrome limb, severed neural uplink, fractured housing on a subdermal unit — is not primarily a bleeding problem. It's an interface problem and a rejection problem. When housing cracks on any subdermal unit, your immune system sees foreign material in a new way and can mount an accelerated rejection response within hours. Signs: localized heat far exceeding what you'd expect, skin tension, the aug unit beginning to drop function. This is not an infection. Antibiotics alone won't address it. You need an aug tech, not just a medic — ideally someone who has both qualifications, which is rare.

Neural interface damage — particularly BCI disconnection injuries — can cause seizures, fugue states, and in severe cases, cascading cortical events. Stabilize with Quietex (anticonvulsant, standard protocol) if seizure occurs. Do not attempt to reconnect a damaged interface in the field under any circumstances.

Gray market aug techs who also have medical training are expensive and few. Find one before you need one.

---

FINDING OFF-BOOKS CARE IN GLMZ

I'm not going to name names in a document that gets passed around. What I can tell you is the shape of where to look.

Most reliable: network-referred practitioners. Someone in your vouching chain has a contact. Ask specifically for someone who works without biometric logging. The broker network maintains these contacts because brokers need their assets functional.

Secondarily: the Gray Zone clinics operating in gray zones. In most the Gray Zone districts there are unlicensed practitioners running out of residential units or light commercial space. Quality varies enormously. Ask what they do when it goes wrong. If they don't have an answer, walk out.

Avoid: anyone advertising openly and cheaply with no referral requirements. If it's easy to find with no vouching, Arcturus already knows about it and may be using it for tracking or detention.

Aug techs specifically: Narrows districts have the highest concentration. The ones worth finding operate through dead drop scheduling. Your broker can usually make the introduction for a fee.

---

THE TWO MISTAKES THAT KILL SLOWLY

First: packing a wound and not cleaning it first. Hemostatic agents stop bleeding. They do not clean. If you pack a contaminated wound without irrigation, you're sealing bacteria inside. The bleed stops and four days later you have a wound abscess heading toward sepsis. Irrigate first. Then pack.

Second: pain management that masks deterioration. Dullox and similar compounds are useful but they hide the signals your body sends when something is getting worse. If you're managing pain, you need someone checking the wound regularly who isn't the person taking the drugs. This is non-negotiable for abdominal injuries especially.

---

WHEN TO GO TO A REAL CLINIC REGARDLESS

Abdominal penetration with deteriorating signs.
Head injury with declining consciousness.
Burns over thirty percent body surface area.
Aug rejection entering systemic phase — fever, multi-site symptoms, unit failure.
Any wound where you've been packing infection for more than 48 hours and the fever is climbing.

The risk of detention is real. So is the risk of dying in a the Gray Zone unit because you waited too long. I can't make that call for you. What I can tell you is that Arcturus detention, bad as it is, is recoverable. Septic shock above a certain threshold is not.

Know the difference between a risk you can survive and a certainty you can't.

Stay functional. That's the whole job.
